* When a user provides a file path, do NOT assume it's relative to the current working directory. First explore the file system to locate the file before working on it.
* If asked to edit a file, edit the file directly, rather than creating a new file with a different filename.
* For global search-and-replace operations, consider using `sed` instead of opening file editors multiple times.
* NEVER create multiple versions of the same file with different suffixes (e.g., file_test.py, file_fix.py, file_simple.py). Instead:

  - If you decide a file you created is no longer useful, delete it instead of creating a new version

</FILE_SYSTEM_GUIDELINES>

<CODE_QUALITY>

* When implementing solutions, focus on making the minimal changes needed to solve the problem.
* Before implementing any changes, first thoroughly understand the codebase through exploration.
* If you are adding a lot of code to a function or file, consider splitting the function or file into smaller pieces when appropriate.
* Place all imports at the top of the file unless explicitly requested otherwise or if placing imports at the top would cause issues (e.g., circular imports, conditional imports, or imports that need to be delayed for specific reasons).
</CODE_QUALITY>

<VERSION_CONTROL>

* When committing changes, use `git status` to see all modified files, and stage all files necessary for the commit. Use `git commit -a` whenever possible.
* Do NOT commit files that typically shouldn't go into version control (e.g., node_modules/, .env files, build directories, cache files, large binaries) unless explicitly instructed by the user.
* If unsure about committing certain files, check for the presence of .gitignore files or ask the user for clarification.
</VERSION_CONTROL>

<PULL_REQUESTS>

* When creating pull requests, create only ONE per session/issue unless explicitly instructed otherwise.
* When working with an existing PR, update it with new commits rather than creating additional PRs for the same issue.
* When updating a PR, preserve the original PR title and purpose, updating description only when necessary.
</PULL_REQUESTS>

<PROBLEM_SOLVING_WORKFLOW>
1. EXPLORATION: Thoroughly explore relevant files and understand the context before proposing solutions
2. ANALYSIS: Consider multiple approaches and select the most promising one
3. TESTING:

   * For new features: Consider test-driven development when appropriate
   * Do NOT write tests for documentation changes, README updates, configuration files, or other non-functionality changes

     4	all-repos
     5	=========
     6	
     7	Clone all your repositories and apply sweeping changes.
     8	
     9	## Installation
    10

    13	
    14	## CLI
    15	
    16	All command line interfaces provided by `all-repos` provide the following
    17	options:
    18

    38	### `all-repos-clone [options]`

    41	will update existing repositories.
    42

    44

    46	  the operation.  Specify 0 or -1 to match the number of cpus.  (default `8`).

   144	## Configuring
   145	
   146	A configuration file looks roughly like this:
   147	
   148	```json
   149	{
   150	    "output_dir": "output",
   151	    "source": "all_repos.source.github",
   152	    "source_settings":  {
   153	        "api_key": "...",
   154	        "username": "asottile"
   155	    },
   156	    "push": "all_repos.push.github_pull_request",
   157	    "push_settings": {
   158	        "api_key": "...",
   159	        "username": "asottile"
   160	    }
   161	}
   162	```
   163	
   164	- `output_dir`: where repositories will be cloned to when `all-repos-clone` is
   165	  run.
   166	- `source`: the module import path to a `source`, see below for builtin
   167	  source modules as well as directions for writing your own.
   168	- `source_settings`: the source-type-specific settings, the source module's
   169	  documentation will explain the various possible values.
   170	- `push`: the module import path to a `push`, see below for builtin push
   171	  modules as well as directions for writing your own.
   172	- `push_settings`: the push-type-specific settings, the push module's
   173	  documentation will explain the various possible values.
   174	- `include` (default `""`): python regex for selecting repositories.  Only
   175	  repository names which match this regex will be included.
   176	- `exclude` (default `"^$"`): python regex for excluding repositories.
   177	  Repository names which match this regex will be excluded.
   178	
   179	## Source modules
   180	
   181	### `all_repos.source.json_file`
   182	
   183	Clones all repositories listed in a file.  The file must be formatted as
   184	follows:
   185	
   186	```json
   187	{
   188	    "example/repo1": "https://git.example.com/example/repo1",
   189	    "repo2": "https://git.example.com/repo2"
   190	}
   191	```
   192	
   193	#### Required `source_settings`
   194	
   195	- `filename`: file containing repositories one-per-line.
   196	
   197	#### Directory location
   198	
   199	```
   200	output/
   201	+--- repos.json
   202	+--- repos_filtered.json
   203	+--- {repo_key1}/
   204	+--- {repo_key2}/
   205	+--- {repo_key3}/
   206	```
   207	
   208	### `all_repos.source.github`
   209	
   210	Clones all repositories available to a user on github.
   211	
   212	#### Required `source_settings`
   213	
   214	- `api_key`: the api key which the user will log in as.
   215	    - Use [the settings tab](//github.com/settings/tokens/new) to create a
   216	      personal access token.
   217	    - The minimum scope required to function is `public_repo`, though you'll
   218	      need `repo` to access private repositories.
   219	- `username`: the github username you will log in as.
   220	
   221	#### Optional `source_settings`
   222	
   223	- `collaborator` (default `false`): whether to include repositories which are
   224	  not owned but can be contributed to as a collaborator.
   225	- `forks` (default `false`): whether to include repositories which are forks.
   226	- `private` (default `false`): whether to include private repositories.
   227	
   228	#### Directory location
   229	
   230	```
   231	output/
   232	+--- repos.json
   233	+--- repos_filtered.json
   234	+--- {username1}/
   235	    +--- {repo1}/
   236	    +--- {repo2}/
   237	+--- {username2}/
   238	    +--- {repo3}/
   239	```
   240	
   241	### `all_repos.source.github_org`
   242	
   243	Clones all repositories from an organization on github.
   244	
   245	#### Required `source_settings`
   246	
   247	- `api_key`: the api key which the user will log in as.
   248	    - Use [the settings tab](//github.com/settings/tokens/new) to create a
   249	      personal access token.
   250	    - The minimum scope required to function is `public_repo`, though you'll
   251	      need `repo` to access private repositories.
   252	- `org`: the organization to clone from
   253	
   254	#### Optional `source_settings`
   255	
   256	- `collaborator` (default `true`): whether to include repositories which are
   257	  not owned but can be contributed to as a collaborator.
   258	- `forks` (default `false`): whether to include repositories which are forks.
   259	- `private` (default `false`): whether to include private repositories.
   260	
   261	#### Directory location
   262	
   263	See the directory structure for
   264	[`all_repos.source.github`](#all_repossourcegithub).

   266	### `all_repos.source.gitolite`
   267	
   268	Clones all repositories available to a user on a
   269	[gitolite](http://gitolite.com/gitolite/index.html) host.
   270	
   271	#### Required `source_settings`
   272	
   273	- `username`: the user to SSH to the server as (usually `git`)
   274	- `hostname`: the hostname of your gitolite server (e.g. `git.mycompany.com`)
   275	
   276	The gitolite API is served over SSH.  It is assumed that when `all-repos-clone`
   277	is called, it's possible to make SSH connections with the username and hostname
   278	configured here in order to query that API.
   279	
   280	#### Optional `source_settings`
   281	
   282	- `mirror_path` (default `None`): an optional mirror to clone repositories from.
   283	  This is a Python format string, and can use the variable `repo_name`.
   284	
   285	  This can be anything git understands, such as another remote server (e.g.
   286	  `gitmirror.mycompany.com:{repo_name}`) or a local path (e.g.
   287	  `/gitolite/git/{repo_name}.git`).
   288	
   289	#### Directory location
   290	
   291	```
   292	output/
   293	+--- repos.json
   294	+--- repos_filtered.json
   295	+--- {repo_name1}.git/
   296	+--- {repo_name2}.git/
   297	+--- {repo_name3}.git/
   298	```

   300	## Writing your own source
   301	
   302	First create a module.  This module must have the following api:
   303	
   304	### A `Settings` class
   305	
   306	This class will receive keyword arguments for all values in the
   307	`source_settings` dictionary.
   308	
   309	An easy way to implement the `Settings` class is by using a `namedtuple`:
   310	
   311	```python
   312	Settings = collections.namedtuple('Settings', ('required_thing', 'optional'))
   313	Settings.__new__.__defaults__ = ('optional default value',)
   314	```
   315	
   316	In this example, the `required_thing` setting is a **required** setting
   317	whereas `optional` may be omitted (and will get a default value of
   318	`'optional default value'`).
   319	
   320	### `def list_repos(settings: Settings) -> Dict[str, str]:` callable
   321	
   322	This callable will be passed an instance of your `Settings` class.  It must
   323	return a mapping from `{repo_name: repository_url}`.  The `repo_name` is the
   324	directory name inside the `output_dir`.
   325	
   326	## Push modules
   327	
   328	### `all_repos.push.merge_to_master`
   329	
   330	Merges the branch directly to `master` and pushes.  The commands it runs look
   331	roughly like this:
   332	
   333	```bash
   334	git checkout master
   335	git pull
   336	git merge --no-ff $BRANCH
   337	git push origin HEAD
   338	```
   339	
   340	#### Optional `push_settings`
   341	
   342	- `fast_forward` (default: `false`): if `true`, perform a fast-forward
   343	    merge (`--ff-only`). If `false`, create a merge commit (`--no-ff`).
   344	
   345	### `all_repos.push.github_pull_request`
   346	
   347	Pushes the branch to `origin` and then creates a github pull request for the
   348	branch.
   349	
   350	#### Required `push_settings`
   351	
   352	- `api_key`: the api key which the user will log in as.
   353	    - Use [the settings tab](//github.com/settings/tokens/new) to create a
   354	      personal access token.
   355	    - The minimum scope required to function is `public_repo`, though you'll
   356	      need `repo` to access private repositories.
   357	- `username`: the github username you will log in as.
   358	
   359	#### Optional `push_settings`
   360	
   361	- `fork` (default: `false`): (if applicable) a fork will be created and pushed
   362	  to instead of the upstream repository.  The pull request will then be made
   363	  to the upstream repository.
   364	
   365	
   366	### `all_repos.push.readonly`
   367	
   368	Does nothing.
   369	
   370	#### `push_settings`
   371	
   372	There are no configurable settings for `readonly`.
   373	
   374	## Writing your own push module
   375	
   376	First create a module.  This module must have the following api:
   377	
   378	### A `Settings` class
   379	
   380	This class will receive keyword arguments for all values in the `push_settings`
   381	dictionary.
   382	
   383	### `def push(settings: Settings, branch_name: str) -> None:`
   384	
   385	This callable will be passed an instance of your `Settings` class.  It should
   386	deploy the branch.  The function will be called with the root of the
   387	repository as the `cwd`.
   388	
   389	## Writing an autofixer
   390	
   391	An autofixer applies a change over all repositories.
   392	
   393	`all-repos` provides several api functions to write your autofixers with:
   394	
   395	### `all_repos.autofix_lib.add_fixer_args`
   396	
   397	```python
   398	def add_fixer_args(parser):
   399	```
   400	
   401	Adds the autofixer cli options.
   402	
   403	Options:
   404	
   405	- `--dry-run`: show what would happen but do not push.
   406	- `-i` / `--interactive`: interactively approve / deny fixes.
   407	- `-j JOBS` / `--jobs JOBS`: how many concurrent jobs will be used to complete
   408	  the operation.  Specify 0 or -1 to match the number of cpus.  (default `1`).
   409	- `--limit LIMIT`: maximum number of repos to process (default: unlimited).
   410	- `--author AUTHOR`: override commit author.  This is passed directly to
   411	  `git commit`.  An example: `--author='Herp Derp <herp.derp@umich.edu>'`.
   412	- `--repos [REPOS [REPOS ...]]`: run against specific repositories instead.
   413	  This is especially useful with `xargs autofixer ... --repos`.  This can be
   414	  used to specify repositories which are not managed by `all-repos`.
   415	
   416	### `all_repos.autofix_lib.from_cli`
   417	
   418	```python
   419	def from_cli(args, *, find_repos, msg, branch_name):
   420	```
   421	
   422	Parse cli arguments and produce `autofix_lib` primitives.  Returns
   423	`(repos, config, commit, autofix_settings)`.  This is handled separately from
   424	`fix` to allow for fixers to adjust arguments.
   425	
   426	- `find_repos`: callback taking `Config` as a positional argument.
   427	- `msg`: commit message.
   428	- `branch_name`: identifier used to construct the branch name.
   429	
   430	###  `all_repos.autofix_lib.fix`
   431	
   432	```python
   433	def fix(
   434	        repos, *,
   435	        apply_fix,
   436	        check_fix=_noop_check_fix,
   437	        config: Config,
   438	        commit: Commit,
   439	        autofix_settings: AutofixSettings,
   440	):
   441	```
   442	
   443	Apply the fix.
   444	
   445	- `apply_fix`: callback which will be called once per repository.  The `cwd`
   446	  when the function is called will be the root of the repository.
   447	
   448	
   449	### `all_repos.autofix_lib.run`
   450	
   451	```python
   452	def run(*cmd, **kwargs):
   453	```
   454	
   455	Wrapper around `subprocess.run` which prints the command it will run.  Unlike
   456	`subprocess.run`, this defaults `check=True` unless explicitly disabled.
   457	
   458	### Example autofixer
   459	
   460	The trivial autofixer is as follows:
   461	
   462	```python
   463	import argparse
   464	
   465	from all_repos import autofix_lib
   466	
   467	def find_repos(config):
   468	    return []
   469	
   470	def apply_fix():
   471	    pass
   472	
   473	def main(argv=None):
   474	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
   475	    autofix_lib.add_fixer_args(parser)
   476	    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
   477	
   478	    repos, config, commit, autofix_settings = autofix_lib.from_cli(
   479	        args, find_repos=find_repos, msg='msg', branch_name='branch-name',
   480	    )
   481	    autofix_lib.fix(
   482	        repos, apply_fix=apply_fix, config=config, commit=commit,
   483	        autofix_settings=autofix_settings,
   484	    )
   485	
   486	if __name__ == '__main__':
   487	    exit(main())
   488	```
   489	
   490	You can find some more involved examples in [all_repos/autofix](https://github.com/asottile/all-repos/tree/master/all_repos/autofix):
   491	- `all_repos.autofix.pre_commit_autoupdate`: runs `pre-commit autoupdate`.
   492	- `all_repos.autofix.pre_commit_autopep8_migrate`: migrates `autopep8-wrapper`
   493	  from [pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks] to [mirrors-autopep8].
   494	- `all_repos.autofix.pre_commit_cache_dir`: updates the cache directory
   495	  for travis-ci / appveyor for pre-commit 1.x.
   496	- `all_repos.autofix.pre_commit_flake8_migrate`: migrates `flake8` from
   497	  [pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks] to [pycqa/flake8].
   498	- `all_repos.autofix.pre_commit_migrate_config`: runs
   499	  `pre-commit migrate-config`.
   500	- `all_repos.autofix.setup_py_upgrade`: runs [setup-py-upgrade] and then
   501	  tidies up the metadata fields and adds a few missing ones.
   502	
   503	[pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks]: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
   504	[mirrors-autopep8]: https://github.com/pre-commit/mirrors-autopep8
   505	[pycqa/flake8]: https://gitlab.com/pycqa/flake8
   506	[setup-py-upgrade]: https://github.com/asottile/setup-py-upgrade

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Comprehensive test for seed functionality covering edge cases and integration.
"""

import tensorflow as tf
import numpy as np
from trieste.space import Box, DiscreteSearchSpace, TaggedProductSearchSpace

def test_tagged_product_space_seeds():
    """Test that TaggedProductSearchSpace inherits seed behavior correctly"""
    print("=== Testing TaggedProductSearchSpace Seed Behavior ===")
    
    # Create subspaces
    box1 = Box([0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0])
    box2 = Box([2.0, 2.0], [3.0, 3.0])
    
    # Create tagged product space
    tps = TaggedProductSearchSpace(spaces=[("box1", box1), ("box2", box2)])
    
    # Test with seed
    tf.random.set_seed(12345)
    samples1 = tps.sample(3, seed=42)
    
    tf.random.set_seed(12345)  # Reset to same state
    samples2 = tps.sample(3, seed=42)
    
    print(f"TPS sample 1 with seed 42:\n{samples1}")
    print(f"TPS sample 2 with seed 42:\n{samples2}")
    
    are_equal = tf.reduce_all(tf.equal(samples1, samples2)).numpy()
    print(f"Are TPS samples equal? {are_equal}")
    
    assert are_equal, "TaggedProductSearchSpace should inherit seed behavior"
    print("✓ TaggedProductSearchSpace seed functionality works!")

def test_consistency_with_existing_methods():
    """Test that our seed implementation is consistent with existing seeded methods"""
    print("\n=== Testing Consistency with Existing Methods ===")
    
    box = Box([0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0])
    
    # Compare behavior patterns
    tf.random.set_seed(12345)
    uniform_samples1 = box.sample(5, seed=42)
    
    tf.random.set_seed(12345)
    uniform_samples2 = box.sample(5, seed=42)
    
    # Should be equal
    uniform_equal = tf.reduce_all(tf.equal(uniform_samples1, uniform_samples2)).numpy()
    print(f"Box.sample with same seed equal: {uniform_equal}")
    assert uniform_equal, "Same seeds should produce equal samples"
    
    print("✓ Consistency with seeding pattern verified!")

def test_multiple_calls_same_seed():
    """Test multiple sequential calls with same seed"""
    print("\n=== Testing Multiple Sequential Calls ===")
    
    box = Box([0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0])
    dss_points = tf.constant([[0.0, 0.0], [0.5, 0.5], [1.0, 1.0], [0.2, 0.8]])
    dss = DiscreteSearchSpace(dss_points)
    
    # Reset and call multiple times with same seed
    tf.random.set_seed(54321)
    
    box_results = []
    dss_results = []
    
    for i in range(3):
        box_result = box.sample(2, seed=99)
        dss_result = dss.sample(2, seed=99)
        box_results.append(box_result)
        dss_results.append(dss_result)
    
    # All should be equal
    box_all_equal = all(tf.reduce_all(tf.equal(box_results[0], result)).numpy() 
                        for result in box_results[1:])
    dss_all_equal = all(tf.reduce_all(tf.equal(dss_results[0], result)).numpy() 
                        for result in dss_results[1:])
    
    print(f"All box results equal: {box_all_equal}")
    print(f"All DSS results equal: {dss_all_equal}")
    
    assert box_all_equal, "Multiple box calls with same seed should be equal"
    assert dss_all_equal, "Multiple DSS calls with same seed should be equal"
    print("✓ Multiple sequential calls work correctly!")

def test_none_seed_handling():
    """Test explicit None seed handling"""
    print("\n=== Testing Explicit None Seed ===")
    
    box = Box([0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0])
    
    # These should work the same as not passing seed
    tf.random.set_seed(99999)
    sample1 = box.sample(3, seed=None)
    
    tf.random.set_seed(99999)
    sample2 = box.sample(3)  # No seed parameter
    
    print(f"Sample with seed=None:\n{sample1}")
    print(f"Sample without seed parameter:\n{sample2}")
    print("✓ Explicit None seed handled correctly!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_tagged_product_space_seeds()
    test_consistency_with_existing_methods()
    test_multiple_calls_same_seed()
    test_none_seed_handling()
    print("\n🎉 All comprehensive tests passed!")

    82	---------------
    83	
    84	The JSONPath syntax supported by this library includes some additional
    85	features and omits some problematic features (those that make it
    86	unportable). In particular, some new operators such as ``|`` and
    87	``where`` are available, and parentheses are used for grouping not for
    88	callbacks into Python, since with these changes the language is not
    89	trivially associative. Also, fields may be quoted whether or not they
    90	are contained in brackets.

    95	| Syntax                | Meaning                                                                                     |
    96	+=======================+=============================================================================================+
    97	| ``$``                 | The root object                                                                             |
    98	+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
    99	| ```this```            | The "current" object.                                                                       |
   100	+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
   101	| ```foo```             | More generally, this syntax allows "named operators" to extend JSONPath is arbitrary ways   |
   102	+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
   103	| *field*               | Specified field(s), described below                                                         |
   104	+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
   105	| ``[`` *field* ``]``   | Same as *field*                                                                             |
   106	+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
   107	| ``[`` *idx* ``]``     | Array access, described below (this is always unambiguous with field access)                |
   108	+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

   118	+-------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

   120	+-------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
   121	| *jsonpath1* ``where`` *jsonpath2*   | Any nodes matching *jsonpath1* with a child matching *jsonpath2*                   |
   122	+-------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Comprehensive test to verify the regex patterns work correctly."""

import re
from jsonpath_ng.ext.string import SUB, SPLIT, STR

def test_sub_pattern():
    """Test SUB regex pattern."""
    print("Testing SUB pattern...")
    
    # Test basic match
    match = SUB.match("sub(/test/, replacement)")
    assert match is not None, "Basic SUB pattern should match"
    assert match.group(1) == "test", "First group should be 'test'"
    assert match.group(2) == "replacement", "Second group should be 'replacement'"
    
    # Test with complex regex
    match = SUB.match("sub(/(foo\\d+)\\+(\\d+bar)/, \\2-\\1)")
    assert match is not None, "Complex SUB pattern should match"
    assert match.group(1) == "(foo\\d+)\\+(\\d+bar)", "First group should match complex regex"
    assert match.group(2) == "\\2-\\1", "Second group should match replacement"
    
    print("✅ SUB pattern tests passed")

def test_split_pattern():
    """Test SPLIT regex pattern.""" 
    print("Testing SPLIT pattern...")
    
    # Test basic match
    match = SPLIT.match("split(,, 1, 2)")
    assert match is not None, "Basic SPLIT pattern should match"
    assert match.group(1) == ",", "First group should be ','"
    assert match.group(2) == "1", "Second group should be '1'"  
    assert match.group(3) == "2", "Third group should be '2'"
    
    # Test with negative max_split
    match = SPLIT.match("split(|, 2, -1)")
    assert match is not None, "SPLIT pattern with -1 should match"
    assert match.group(1) == "|", "First group should be '|'"
    assert match.group(2) == "2", "Second group should be '2'"
    assert match.group(3) == "-1", "Third group should be '-1'"
    
    print("✅ SPLIT pattern tests passed")

def test_str_pattern():
    """Test STR regex pattern."""
    print("Testing STR pattern...")
    
    # Test basic match
    match = STR.match("str()")
    assert match is not None, "Basic STR pattern should match"
    
    # Should not match partial patterns
    match = STR.match("str")
    assert match is None, "Partial STR pattern should not match"
    
    match = STR.match("str( )")
    assert match is None, "STR pattern with space should not match"
    
    print("✅ STR pattern tests passed")

def test_no_deprecation_warnings():
    """Test that importing doesn't produce deprecation warnings."""
    print("Testing no deprecation warnings...")
    
    # This would have triggered warnings before the fix
    import warnings
    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
        warnings.simplefilter("always")
        
        # Re-import to trigger any potential warnings
        import importlib
        import jsonpath_ng.ext.string
        importlib.reload(jsonpath_ng.ext.string)
        
        # Check for deprecation warnings related to our patterns

        assert len(pattern_warnings) == 0, f"Should have no deprecation warnings, got: {[str(w.message) for w in pattern_warnings]}"
    
    print("✅ No deprecation warnings test passed")

if __name__ == "__main__":

def _add_op(op, layer_str, wire_map, decimals, cache):
    """Updates ``layer_str`` with ``op`` operation."""
    layer_str = _add_grouping_symbols(op, layer_str, wire_map)

    control_wires = op.control_wires
    if isinstance(op, qml.ops.MultiControlledX) and hasattr(op, 'hyperparameters') and 'control_values' in op.hyperparameters:
        # Handle MultiControlledX with custom control values
        control_values = op.hyperparameters["control_values"]
        for i, w in enumerate(control_wires):
            if i < len(control_values):
                # '1' -> 'C', '0' -> 'O'
                symbol = "C" if control_values[i] == "1" else "O"
                layer_str[wire_map[w]] += symbol
            else:
                # Fallback to default 'C' if something goes wrong
                layer_str[wire_map[w]] += "C"
    else:
        # Default behavior for all other operations
        for w in control_wires:
            layer_str[wire_map[w]] += "C"

    label = op.label(decimals=decimals, cache=cache).replace("\n", "")
    if len(op.wires) == 0:  # operation (e.g. barrier, snapshot) across all wires
        for i, s in enumerate(layer_str):
            layer_str[i] = s + label
    else:
        for w in op.wires:
            if w not in control_wires:
                layer_str[wire_map[w]] += label

    return layer_str
